The summary of Block Diffusion RooflinesPrevious: IntroductionNext: 1 · Setup and the gain

Our main throughput result

We start by giving our main result, which is a compact formula for the throughput gain of TD over AR. Of course, this formula is idealized, as it holds under some critical assumptions, but we will see that it can faithfully act as a guiding north star while navigating TD and AR inference.

You can click on any formula to see a definition of the symbols it uses.

\[ \Gamma \;=\; \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min\bigl(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}},\,I^\star\bigr)}{\min\bigl(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\,I^\star\bigr)},\qquad \omega = S\,r + 1 \]

Proposition 1, the result of Part 1. Every symbol is defined on the Symbols page.

In the equations, AR quantities are in blue and TD quantities in orange, as in the figures.

Main take-aways 🏠
  1. TD trades bytes for FLOPs. A canvas of \(b\) tokens costs \(\omega\) forward passes instead of one, so TD does \(\omega\) times more FLOPs per token than AR. In return, every byte it reads from HBM serves \(b\) positions instead of one.
  2. The best batch is the one at which a TD pass just becomes compute-bound. At smaller batches TD is still memory-bound, and the gain grows as a larger batch lowers the linear penalty. At larger batches TD already runs at peak while AR keeps speeding up, so the gain falls.
  3. At long context the batch stops mattering. When the cache bytes of a sequence far exceed its share of the weight bytes, only the attention matters to establish rooflines and the linear part can be ignored. In that case TD shines since each of its passes reads the KV cache once, just like an AR step, but serves \(b\) queries instead of one.
  4. A higher ridge point means more to gain. Whenever TD is compute-bound and AR is not, the gain scales linearly with \(I^\star\). However, TD then needs more to reach the ridge: a larger batch at short context, and a canvas longer than \(I^\star/I_{\mathrm{attn}}\) at long context.

The three regimes that occur

The formula above involves the ratio of two minima, which leads to four possible scenarios. Since, under reasonable assumptions, \(I_{\mathrm{TD}} \geq I_{\mathrm{AR}}\) (Corollary 1), only three regimes occur.

AR compute-bound
\(\Gamma = 1/\omega\)

TD is then compute-bound as well. Both run at peak, and TD does \(\omega\) times the work. In that scenario, using TD is strictly worse. However, this scenario is extremely rare, as we will see.

Both passes run at the peak, so time is FLOPs, and a canvas spends \(\omega\) times AR's FLOPs per token: \(\Gamma \le 1/\omega\), equal to it under Proposition 1. We claim that this setting is unrealistic, but just how unrealistic is it? AR becomes compute-bound at

\[ \begin{gathered} \class{mj-ar}{B^\star_{AR}} = \frac{I^\star s_wW_{\mathrm{tot}}}{2N_{\mathrm{act}}}\\[4pt] = \frac{206 \times 2 \times 24.5\text{B}}{2 \times 3.08\text{B}} \approx 1{,}640. \end{gathered} \]

This is with zero context \(C\)! The batch that AR needs grows with the context, and there is usually even a point beyond which no batch size renders AR compute-bound. For instance, by Proposition 8, beyond about 135 tokens of context no batch makes an AR step compute-bound.

Both memory-bound
\(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\)

TD's extra FLOPs add no time. Each read of the weights and of the KV cache serves TPF tokens, divided by the penalty \(\Pi\): the linear (MoE) penalty, the attention (sparse) penalty, or a byte-weighted mix of the two (Proposition 2).

Per sequence, an AR step reads \(\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}\) bytes for one token; a canvas reads \(\omega\) times \(\class{mj-td}{Q^{TD}} = \Pi\,\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}\) for \(b\) tokens. Both passes are memory-bound, so the gain is the ratio of these bytes per token:

\[ \Gamma = \frac{\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}}{\omega\,\Pi\,\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}}/b} = \frac{\mathrm{TPF}}{\Pi}. \]
AR memory-, TD compute-bound
\(\Gamma = \dfrac{I^\star}{\omega\,\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}}\)

This quantity decreases with the batch \(B\), as \(1/B\) once AR touches every expert; the gain rises with the batch only in the previous regime. At long context, it tends to \(I^\star/(\omega I_{\mathrm{attn}})\), which is at least 1 whenever \(\omega I_{\mathrm{attn}} \le I^\star\): 1.72 on an H200.

TD runs at the peak FLOP rate \(\pi\) and AR at \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\,\beta\), so TD computes \(I^\star/\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) times faster than AR but does \(\omega\) times as many FLOPs per token; the ratio of the two is the formula above. At short context, \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\) grows with the batch. At long context, \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}} \to I_{\mathrm{attn}}\), and at any batch we have

\[ \Gamma \to \frac{I^\star}{\omega\,I_{\mathrm{attn}}} = \frac{206}{15 \times 8} = 1.72. \]

The above suggests that at long context, TD is (almost) always better than AR when it comes to throughput.

Critical hyperparameters

While the main throughput formula and the four main take-aways give high-level ideas on when TD is advantageous over AR, it is also interesting to identify the main hyperparameters of the model and of the serving that decide which paradigm is worth it.

Canvas cost, \(\omega\)

A canvas costs \(\omega = Sr+1\) forward passes. This is what hurts TD, as the gain is inversely proportional to \(\omega\).

\[ \begin{gathered} \omega = S\,r + 1,\\[4pt] \Gamma = \frac{1}{\omega}\cdot\frac{\min(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}},\,I^\star)}{\min(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\,I^\star)}. \end{gathered} \]

The canvas cost \(\omega\) corresponds to \(S\) denoising passes, each one costing \(r\) forward passes (\(r \lt 1\) for a smaller denoiser), and one commit pass that writes the canvas to the KV cache. The intensity of a pass does not depend on \(S\), so under Proposition 1 the gain is proportional to \(1/\omega\).

Canvas length, \(b\)

This is what makes TD worth it. While TD is memory-bound, the gain grows linearly with \(b\).

\[ \begin{gathered} \mathrm{TPF} = \frac{b}{\omega},\qquad \class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} = \frac{b}{\Pi}\,\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}},\\[4pt] \class{mj-td}{B^\star_{TD}} \approx \frac{I^\star s_w\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}}{2b\,N_{\mathrm{act}}}. \end{gathered} \]

While a TD pass is memory-bound, i.e., \(\class{mj-td}{I_{TD}} \leq I^\star\), we have that \(\Gamma = \mathrm{TPF}/\Pi\) and therefore the gain grows linearly with \(b\). Once it is compute-bound, \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\) no longer depends on \(b\). Additionally, a longer canvas reaches that regime at a smaller batch1.

Linear penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\)

At small batches, TD has to load more experts from memory than AR. This lowers the gain.

\[ \begin{gathered} \Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}(B) = \frac{\class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B)}{\class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B)},\\[4pt] \class{mj-ar}{W_{AR}}(B) = W_{\mathrm{ne}} + L\,U_{E,k}(B)\,W^e,\\[2pt] \class{mj-td}{W_{TD}}(B) = W_{\mathrm{ne}} + L\,U_{E,k}(Bb)\,W^e,\\[4pt] U_{E,k}(N) = E\Bigl[1 - \bigl(1 - \tfrac{k}{E}\bigr)^{N}\Bigr]. \end{gathered} \]

\(U_{E,k}(N)\) is the expected number of distinct experts that \(N\) positions touch in one layer. A TD step routes \(Bb\) positions, and an AR step routes \(B\) positions and touches about \(kB\) experts. The dense part \(W_{\mathrm{ne}}\) is read by both and dilutes the penalty incurred by TD. Dense models have \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}} = 1\). The penalty \(\Pi_{\mathrm{lin}}\) divides the gain when both TD and AR are memory-bound. Hence the effect is mostly felt at small batch sizes.

Attention penalty, \(\Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}\)

Similarly, when global layers are replaced by sparse ones, TD pays a larger price, i.e., it loads more of the KV cache than AR. Overall, sparsity affects TD more than AR.

\[ \begin{gathered} \Pi_{\mathrm{attn}}(C) - 1 = \frac{\nu_S\,\bigl[\,U_{C,m}(b) - m\,\bigr]}{\class{mj-ar}{Q^{AR}_{\mathrm{attn}}}(C)},\\[4pt] U_{C,m}(b) = C\Bigl[1 - \bigl(1 - \tfrac{m}{C}\bigr)^{b}\Bigr] \quad (C \ge m). \end{gathered} \]

This is the counterpart of the linear penalty on the attention side, when the attention is sparse. Each query selects its own \(m\) cached tokens. A TD step reads \(U_{C,m}(b)\) tokens (up to \(\min(bm, C)\)), while an AR step reads only \(m\) (since there is only one query). The penalty is 1 while \(C \le m\), largest for \(m \lt C \lesssim bm\), and returns to 1 as \(C \to \infty\), since the union saturates at \(bm\) while the AR attention bytes grow linearly in \(C\) because of the indexer scan.

Batch, \(B\)

A larger batch raises the arithmetic intensity of both TD and AR. However, once a pass is compute-bound, raising the batch no longer speeds it up. Since TD becomes compute-bound before AR, large batches generally lower the gain.

\[ Q^{X}(B, C) = \underbrace{\frac{s_wW_X(B)}{B}}_{\text{weights}} + \underbrace{Q^{X}_{\mathrm{attn}}(C)}_{\text{cache}}. \]

For \(X \in \{AR, TD\}\), the weights are shared by the batch and each sequence has its own cache. A larger batch divides the weight bytes per sequence and leaves the cache bytes unchanged. So raising the batch size raises the intensity of both AR and TD. At first it helps TD more, due to the linear MoE penalty. But once TD is compute-bound, it only raises \(\class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}}\), and \(\Gamma = I^\star/(\omega \class{mj-ar}{I_{AR}})\) falls.

Context, \(C\)

As the context grows, the arithmetic intensity of the model tends to that of the attention. This generally favours TD, whose attention intensity is \(b\) times that of AR.

\[ \begin{gathered} I_X = \theta^X_{\mathrm{lin}}\,I^X_{\mathrm{lin}} + \theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}}\,I^X_{\mathrm{attn}},\\[4pt] \theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}} = \frac{Q^X_{\mathrm{attn}}}{Q^X}. \end{gathered} \]

Each intensity (TD or AR) is the weighted average of its two parts, linear and attention (Proposition 2). As \(C\) grows, the attention share \(\theta^X_{\mathrm{attn}}\) goes to 1 and the intensity of the model is roughly the intensity of the attention. Without sparse layers, the arithmetic intensity of the attention of TD is \(b\) times that of AR, and therefore long contexts favour TD.

What the formulas leave out

The gains above are roofline bounds under the assumptions (A1)–(A5) of Proposition 1. What these assumptions leave out (the vocabulary, kernel-by-kernel timing, kernel efficiency, correlated routing and a few smaller effects) is listed in Part 1.

Notes

  1. One trade-off that we deliberately leave out of the analysis is that the longer the canvas, the harder it is for TD to reach the quality of AR. ↩
